newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean firms flock to Hanbo pre-auction session.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean firms flock to Hanbo pre-auction session.

text.p: South Korean creditors and companies turned out in force on Tuesday to find out how to snare a piece of failed Hanbo Steel Co, a key creditor said.

Representatives from the Hyundai Group and 10 other powerful South Korean conglomerates participated in a session at which plans to auction Hanbo on July 8 were outlined, said main creditor Korea First Bank.
The government is believed to favour a takeover by Hyundai Group, and has urged it to so instead of building a new mill.

But the group has repeatedly said it was not interested in taking over Hanbo Steel despite its interest in steelmaking. Still, senior officials from Hyundai Heavy Industries and Inchon and Iron Steel showed up at the session.

A Korea First Bank official said about 130 officials from creditors and companies attended the pre-auction session, at which it was explained how the auction would work, including details on financing and buyer qualifications.

After analysing qualifications of possible candidates to take over Hanbo Steel, Korea First Bank and other creditor banks had issued invitations to 17 groups, including the nation's powerful Hyundai, Samsung, LG and Daewoo groups, as well as POSCO.
According to the strict qualifications established by the creditors, only 17 groups were deemed eligible to take over the troubled Hanbo Steel, which was declared insolvent on January.
The creditors demanded potential buyers each have a minimum one trillion won of shareholders' equity and a minimum 10 trillion won of assets and annual turnover.
Six other invitees, including Sunkyong Group, Hanjin Group HANJ.CN and Lotte Group, which are among the top 30 business conglomerates or chaebols, did not attend.
Creditors decided to put Hanbo Steel on the auction block after they received reports from the Seoul-based accounting firm of Ahn, Kwon and Co on their assessment of Hanbo's assets and liabilities.
The steelmaker's liabilities were estimated at 6.61 trillion won, compared to assets of 4.97 trillion.

The Korea First Bank official said creditors would reduce the financial burden for the entity that takes over Hanbo by delaying interest payments on the liabilities, which carried an annual interest rate of 11.5 percent.

In the first 10 years, the acquiring company would be allowed to pay interest of 8.5 percent, the prime lending rate. After that creditors would let the acquirer to pay the 3 percentage point difference in interest over five years after a 10-year grace period. The Korea First Bank official said candidates should clarify in their bids how much of Hanbo's liabilities they would assume. The steel mill, which is 90 percent complete, is expected to make a profit.
They also said potential buyers should submit a plan outlining when and how they would increase Hanbo Steel's capital.

Hanbo's creditors had taken over 26.5 percent of Hanbo shares from the founder Chung Tae-soo and his family after Hanbo defaulted on debt payments. The steelmaker's failure rocked the country's financial markets and revealed a huge loans-for-kickback scandal.
